claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the interplay between atomic size mismatch and enthalpy of mixing.
Atomic size mismatch and enthalpy of mixing determine the thermodynamic stability of the resulting alloy nanoparticles.
Atomic size mismatch and enthalpy of mixing determine kinetic pathways leading to alloying rather than phase separation.
Selecting different combinations of noble metals and other elements can vary atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy.
Atomic-scale interactions in these systems include lattice strain and element-specific chemical-bonding preferences.
Atomic size mismatch introduces lattice strain.
Lattice strain competes with enthalpy-of-mixing effects to determine homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation.
Larger atomic size mismatches promote elemental segregation.
Unfavorable mixing enthalpies promote elemental segregation.
Smaller atomic size mismatches stabilize a high-entropy alloy structure.
Favorable mixing enthalpies stabilize a high-entropy alloy structure.
Systems combining smaller atomic size mismatch with more negative mixing enthalpy will form homogeneous high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Systems combining smaller atomic size mismatch with more negative mixing enthalpy will preserve surface-atom exposure.
Systems combining larger atomic size mismatch with less negative or positive mixing enthalpy will undergo phase separation or elemental segregation.
The proposed relationship applies to noble metal–based systems containing up to seven elements.
For systems with extreme atomic size mismatch or highly positive mixing enthalpy, phase separation is inevitable.
